analysis.one_liner: Permanently bans new offshore oil and gas drilling off Florida's coasts.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to permanently ban new offshore drilling within 125 miles of Florida's coast died in committee without a vote, despite 21 cosponsors split evenly between Republicans and Democrats.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would write a permanent ban into federal law against offering any new oil and gas leases in three areas: the eastern Gulf of Mexico within 125 miles of Florida's shoreline, the South Atlantic planning area south of a line near the Florida-Georgia border, and the Straits of Florida. It would not cancel any drilling leases already issued. It never received a committee or floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Florida's coastal residents, beachgoers, and the tourism and fishing businesses that depend on clean water and intact beaches. A permanent statutory ban would protect them from the risk of new offshore drilling and oil spills in the eastern Gulf, the South Atlantic, and the Straits of Florida, and would prevent any future administration from simply lifting a temporary protections by executive action, because this ban would be written into the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act itself.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Florida coastal communities and beach economies

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits the federal government from offering any tract for oil and gas leasing or preleasing in the Eastern Gulf of Mexico within 125 miles of Florida's coastline, the South Atlantic Planning Area south of 30 degrees 43 minutes North Latitude, and the Straits of Florida Planning Area.

Writes the ban directly into the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act, stating it applies 'notwithstanding any other provision of this section or any other law' — meaning a future administration could not lift it the way a temporary presidential withdrawal or an expiring moratorium can be lifted.

Keeps drilling activity — and with it the risk of a spill that could close beaches and damage fisheries for years — away from Florida's shoreline, where tourism and commercial fishing are major parts of the coastal economy.

analysis.who_pays: The offshore oil and gas industry, which would lose access to three large planning areas off Florida for new leases. The federal treasury would forgo any future bonus bids and royalties those leases might have generated, and the country would forgo whatever oil and gas could have been produced there. No consumer price effect would be immediate, since the bill does not touch any existing lease.

drawbacks.text: It removes three large offshore areas from potential energy production and from federal leasing revenue, at a time when national production levels are a live policy question.

The practical change was narrower than the headline: the bill explicitly does not affect any lease already issued, and it would have codified protections that largely already existed — the areas it bars include the zones Congress already put off-limits in the 2006 Gulf of Mexico Energy Security Act, so much of its effect was making temporary protection permanent rather than opening-to-closed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For Floridians the benefit is real but partly defensive: the bill converts existing and temporary protections into permanent law, which matters most after 2022 when the statutory eastern Gulf moratorium expires. The cost — foregone drilling and lease revenue in the eastern Gulf, South Atlantic, and Straits of Florida — falls on the oil industry and the federal treasury, and the drafting limits its impact by leaving existing leases untouched. It is a modest, well-targeted bill whose main weakness is that it died before anyone could weigh it.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee, got a single subcommittee hearing, and quietly died when the Congress ended without ever coming up for a vote.

narrative.text: Representative Kathy Castor introduced the bill on April 26, 2021, joined by 19 other members of the Florida delegation, including Republicans such as Vern Buchanan, Gus Bilirakis, Matt Gaetz, Byron Donalds, and Mario Diaz-Balart's fellow Floridians Brian Mast and Bill Posey — a genuinely bipartisan Florida-delegation roster.

It went to the House Committee on Natural Resources on the day it was introduced, was sent to the Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee on May 10, and the subcommittee held a hearing on May 13, 2021.

After that hearing, no further action was ever recorded: the committee never voted on the bill, the House never debated it, and no Senate companion appears in its history. The bill expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The offshore oil and gas industry is better off, because it kept future leasing options off Florida's coast alive once the temporary statutory moratorium expires; no member of Congress ever had to cast a recorded vote against a bipartisan Florida coastal-protection bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Offshore drilling interests and untouched incumbents

for.name: Kathy Castor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled a bipartisan group of 19 fellow Florida House members as original cosponsors.

for.name: 11 House Republicans from Florida
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the drilling ban, including Vern Buchanan, Gus Bilirakis, Matt Gaetz, Byron Donalds, C. Scott Franklin, Brian Mast, Bill Posey, John Rutherford, Maria Elvira Salazar, Carlos Gimenez, and Michael Waltz-era colleagues listed on the bill.

for.name: 10 House Democrats from Florida
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Charlie Crist, Val Demings, Ted Deutch, Lois Frankel, Al Lawson, Stephanie Murphy, Darren Soto, Debbie Wasserman Schultz, and Frederica Wilson.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee leadership
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over offshore leasing
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the May 2021 subcommittee hearing; never scheduled a markup or committee vote, letting the bill expire.

sides.party_line_note: All 21 cosponsors were Florida House members split 11 Republicans and 10 Democrats, and the bill died from committee inaction rather than any recorded vote, since no chamber vote ever took place.

industries.note: The bill permanently closes three planning areas off Florida to new leasing and preleasing, eliminating future access worth potential bids and royalties to the industry. Its interest in keeping those waters open runs against coastal communities that bear the spill risk.

Beach towns, hotels, charter fishing, and related businesses depend on coastlines unpolluted by a spill; a permanent leasing ban lowers that risk for the eastern Gulf, South Atlantic, and Straits of Florida.
Gulf and South Atlantic fisheries, which an oil spill could close or damage for years, gain the same permanent protection from new drilling activity near Florida's shelf.
